rationale: This qualitative study (coding of 9 Ugandan national water/decentralization laws and policies alongside 93 semi-structured interviews with political and technical local government officials across 22 sub-counties in 3 districts) examines how regulative, normative, and cultural-cognitive institutions shape local government fulfillment of rural water mandates under Uganda's 2019 National O&M Framework. The central empirical mechanism family is institutional_structure_coordination: the allocation of infrastructure development, contracting, monitoring, and regulatory mandates across decentralized district and sub-county tiers, constrained by centralized intergovernmental fiscal transfers (delayed/insufficient central funding releases) and weak coordination from NGOs and implementers. Delegated management via contracted Area Service Providers replacing community-based management (regulatory_model_ownership) defines the policy shift, alongside secondary themes of informal politician-financed repairs/workarounds (discretion_accommodation), user tariff/enrollment-fee collection and subsidies (fees_tariffs_subsidies), and community sensitization/water user committees (participation_assistance). The primary empirical outcome analyzed is administrative_outcome—specifically, local government actors' compliance with and fulfillment of assigned governance, administrative, regulatory, and service-delivery support mandates (with borehole functional sustainability as the motivating downstream goal rather than a directly measured water-point outcome).
